about: The twelve regional profile cards of Learn (curriculum v2 §15): one structure for every card (system structure, institutions, main challenges, distinctive research questions, verified key numbers, as-of date). Ten cards come from the course's field-landscape survey, whose numbers were each opened on the cited page on 2 November 2026; the Plains (SPP) and Australia cards were verified on their primary sources on 7 November 2026. Ember is cited as a compiler of official statistics. No ranking of regions and no verdict on any policy.

cards.title: United States
structure: Seven ISO/RTO markets, plus vertically integrated utilities in much of the Southeast and West.
Three weakly coupled interconnections.
Gas is the largest source of electricity; demand is rising again with data centers, manufacturing and electrification.
institutions: FERC: wholesale markets and interstate transmission.
NERC: reliability standards.
DOE and EIA: research, policy and statistics.
State utility commissions: retail rates.
ISOs and RTOs: grid operation and markets.
challenges: A long interconnection backlog, and who pays for new transmission.
Adequacy as large loads arrive and older plants retire.
questions: How much capacity can flexible large loads save?
Do the cluster-study reforms after FERC Order 2023 shorten the time to operation?
What does transmission between regions buy in extreme cold?

numbers.text: About 2,061 GW seeking interconnection at the end of 2025: 1,312 GW of generation and about 749 GW of storage.
Wind and utility-scale solar made 17% of 2025's generation; 19% with small-scale solar.
Data centers used 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023 (176 TWh).

cards.title: The Plains (SPP region)
cards.note: Prairie Town's real-data home: the course's hourly shapes come from this grid.
structure: A regional transmission organization (RTO): it runs the bulk grid and the wholesale market for its members.
One market since 1 March 2014, the Integrated Marketplace: day-ahead and real-time energy, reserves and congestion rights.
At the western edge of the Eastern Interconnection, between MISO to the east and ERCOT to the south.
institutions: SPP: reliability coordination, scheduling, transmission planning and the wholesale market.
FERC: granted SPP its RTO status in 2004.
SPP's Market Monitoring Unit: an independent monitor that reports on the market each year.
Members: generation-and-transmission cooperatives, municipal systems, investor-owned utilities, independent transmission companies and power producers.
challenges: Congestion and wind curtailment: average hourly curtailment rose from 136 MW in 2019 to 1,097 MW in 2023.
Winter adequacy and fuel supply: in February 2021 SPP cut regional demand twice, the first region-wide curtailments in its history.
In 2025, rising gas prices, load growth and resource adequacy concerns.
questions: How much does new transmission cut wind curtailment and congestion?
How should capacity be accredited when cold weather takes out many plants and their fuel at once?
How should wind forecast uncertainty enter the day-ahead commitment?

numbers.text: 161 members in all or part of 17 states, about 732,086 square miles; among them 26 generation-and-transmission cooperatives, 18 municipal systems and 16 investor-owned utilities.
Wind made 36.7% of the 300,382 GWh produced in 2025, more than coal (29%) or gas (25.1%).
Wind capacity 35,934 MW at the end of 2025.
Peak 58.0 GW on 27 July 2026, a record; the earlier peak was 56.0 GW on 21 August 2023.
February 2021: demand cut by about 1.5% for 50 minutes on 15 February and about 6.5% for about three hours on 16 February.

cards.title: European Union
structure: Unbundled zonal markets, coupled day-ahead and intraday.
Dense interconnection between countries.
Nuclear power, led by France; wind; fast-growing solar.
Flat demand overall, with clusters of data-center load.
institutions: European Commission (DG ENER): energy law and policy.
ACER: cooperation of national regulators.
ENTSO-E: the transmission operators' network and grid plans.
National regulators and TSOs; Eurostat for statistics.
challenges: Negative prices and falling solar capture prices.
questions: How does bidding-zone design affect redispatch?
Which mix of storage, demand response and interconnection cuts negative-price hours most?
Which connection rules fit clusters of data-center load?

numbers.text: Renewables made 47.5% of gross electricity consumption in 2024 (Austria 90.1%, Malta 10.7%).
Wind and solar made 30% of 2025's electricity, above fossil fuels at 29%.
Data centers used 23% of Ireland's metered electricity in 2025 (5% in 2015).

cards.title: China
structure: State-owned grid companies; dispatch largely by province.
Spot markets moving toward a unified national market; market pricing for new wind and solar since 2025.
Ultra-high-voltage (UHV) lines carry power from west to east; coal still leads generation.
institutions: NDRC and NEA: planning, prices and energy regulation.
State Grid and China Southern Power Grid.
China Electricity Council; the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Beijing and Guangzhou power exchanges.
challenges: Rising curtailment of wind and solar.
Coal plants retrofitted for flexibility, and capacity payments.
questions: How do provincial spot designs affect how much wind and solar is used?
Which mix of UHV lines, storage and flexible coal keeps utilisation at or above 90% at least cost?
How does market pricing change where wind and solar are built?

numbers.text: 317 GW of solar added in 2025; utilisation 95% for solar and 94% for wind.
Solar capacity 1,286 GW at the end of July 2026, passing coal at 1,285 GW.
Fossil fuels made 58% of 2025's electricity; wind and solar 22%.

cards.title: India
structure: State distribution companies (DISCOMs) buy power under long-term contracts.
One synchronous national grid.
Coal makes most of the electricity, while most capacity is now non-fossil; the evening peak binds.
institutions: Ministry of Power and the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE).
Central Electricity Authority (CEA).
CERC and state commissions: regulation and tariffs.
Grid-India (operator), CTUIL (transmission planning) and SECI (renewable tenders).
challenges: The evening peak in a solar-heavy system.
Transmission and storage for the Rajasthan and Gujarat renewable zones.
questions: How much storage does each step in solar's share need?
How do solar-powered farm feeders and time-of-day tariffs reshape load?
Does market coupling outperform bilateral contracts?

numbers.text: Non-fossil capacity 300.50 GW, over 54% of about 552 GW, on 31 July 2026.
Fossil fuels made 73% of 2025's electricity; solar 9.4%.

cards.title: Japan and South Korea
structure: Japan: ten areas, split between 50 Hz and 60 Hz, joined by limited converters; liberalised retail, a power exchange (JEPX) and a capacity market.
South Korea: one network and retail company (KEPCO) and a cost-based pool (KPX).
Both are isolated systems that import their fuels; nuclear plays a large role in both.
institutions: Japan: METI and its energy agency (ANRE), OCCTO (cross-regional coordination), the Nuclear Regulation Authority, JEPX.
South Korea: the energy ministry (MOTIE), KEPCO, KPX.
challenges: Curtailment and weak links between regions (Kyushu, Jeju).
questions: What would more 50/60 Hz converter capacity save?
How should South Korea plan southwest offshore wind together with lines to Seoul?
LNG storage or batteries as a hedge for supply security?

numbers.text: Japan, 2025: fossil fuels 67% of electricity, solar 10%, nuclear 9%.
South Korea, 2025: fossil fuels 60% of electricity; wind and solar 7%.

cards.title: Nordic countries
structure: Nord Pool bidding zones; flow-based market coupling since October 2024; dense HVDC links.
Hydro in Norway and Sweden, wind in Denmark.
Sweden and Finland also run nuclear plants.
New industrial, hydrogen and data-center loads; district heating in many cities.
institutions: Grid operators: Statnett, Svenska kraftnät, Fingrid, Energinet.
National regulators.
Nord Pool: the power exchange.
Statistics Norway (SSB) and Eurostat: statistics.
questions: How has flow-based coupling changed price spreads?
How should the value of stored water be modelled as wind grows?
What flexibility can district heating give?

numbers.text: Norway, 2025: 161.8 TWh generated, hydro 89.9%, a record net export of 22.8 TWh.
Renewables' share of gross electricity consumption in 2024: Sweden 88.1%, Denmark 79.7%, Finland 54.3%.

cards.title: Gulf states
structure: Vertically integrated state utilities; single buyers contract independent power producers and power-and-water plants.
Oman runs a spot market; the GCC Interconnection Authority links all six states.
Gas and oil make most electricity, with large solar tenders.
The UAE also runs a nuclear plant.
institutions: Saudi Arabia: Ministry of Energy, the regulator SERA, Saudi Electricity Company.
UAE: Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure, DEWA, EWEC.
Qatar's KAHRAMAA; Oman's regulator APSR.
The GCC Interconnection Authority (GCCIA).
challenges: The value of oil burned for power that could be sold.
Subsidised tariffs, and power and water plants that run together.
questions: How should power and water be planned together with solar and storage?
How much peak can district cooling and thermal storage shave?
What is reserve sharing through the GCCIA worth?

numbers.text: Saudi Arabia: 98% of electricity from fossil fuels; demand per person 3.5 times the world average (data year not stated).
UAE: 68% from fossil fuels; demand per person 4.2 times the world average (data year not stated).

cards.title: Sub-Saharan Africa
structure: Mostly vertically integrated state utilities; Nigeria unbundled in 2013, and South Africa's Eskom is unbundling.
Thin regional power pools (SAPP, WAPP, EAPP, CAPP).
Hydro in many countries, coal in South Africa; diesel and off-grid solar where the grid does not reach.
institutions: National utilities and regulators.
The regional power pools.
The African Development Bank, the World Bank and AUDA-NEPAD.
challenges: Climate risk to hydro; a high cost of capital.
questions: Where is grid extension, a mini-grid or a solar home system the least-cost way to connect people?
What is regional trade worth when river flows vary?
Which tariffs make mini-grids viable?

numbers.text: 655 million people worldwide without electricity, over 560 million of them in Sub-Saharan Africa.
South Africa, 2025: 83% of electricity from fossil fuels; wind and solar 13%.

cards.title: Latin America
structure: Brazil: a hydro-dominated national grid (the SIN), cost-based dispatch, auctions plus a free market.
Chile: liberalised, with cost-based dispatch on a grid about 3,000 km long.
Mexico: the state utility CFE dominates after the 2025 reform.
institutions: Brazil: MME, the regulator ANEEL, the operator ONS, the planner EPE, the trading chamber CCEE.
Chile: the energy commission CNE and the operator CEN.
Mexico: SENER, the operator CENACE, CFE.
OLADE, the regional energy organisation.
challenges: Curtailment and transmission bottlenecks in northern Chile.
questions: How should reservoirs be run together with wind and solar under drought (stochastic dual dynamic programming)?
Which storage and transmission cut Chile's curtailment most cheaply?
How do compensation rules for rooftop and other distributed generation shift costs?

numbers.text: Brazil, 2025: hydro 52% of electricity, wind and solar 27%, clean sources 89%.
Chile: 20,483.5 MW of non-conventional renewable capacity out of 39,104.4 MW installed, November 2025.
Mexico, 2025: 74% of electricity from fossil fuels; wind and solar 13%.

cards.title: Small island systems
structure: One integrated utility per island.
Small, isolated grids with little inertia.
Imported diesel and fuel oil; high shares of rooftop solar.
institutions: Hawaii's Public Utilities Commission and State Energy Office.
CARICOM's Energy Unit and CCREEE (Caribbean).
The Pacific Community, PCREEE and the Pacific Power Association.
IRENA's SIDS Lighthouses initiative.
challenges: Stability at very high shares of inverter-based power.
questions: How much grid-forming capacity does a grid that runs almost entirely on inverters need?
Which mix of solar, storage and diesel holds up under fuel-price and storm risk?
How should rooftop export tariffs work once midday solar exceeds load?

numbers.text: Hawaii's average retail price was 38.00 cents per kWh in 2024, the highest of any state; the U.S. average was 12.94.
Hawaii had the highest average residential bill in the U.S. in 2024: $213 a month.

cards.title: Australia
structure: The National Electricity Market (NEM): one wholesale market across Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania.
Western Australia runs its own Wholesale Electricity Market.
Millions of rooftop solar systems; grid-scale batteries growing fast.
institutions: AEMO: independent market and system operator and system planner for the NEM and Western Australia's market.
The Clean Energy Regulator: runs the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme for rooftop systems, which ends in 2030.
State governments and distribution network businesses: emergency backstops that can turn rooftop solar down.
challenges: Minimum system load on sunny, mild days, typically in autumn and spring.
Keeping enough essential system services as large spinning generators run less.
Evening peaks (4 pm to 9 pm), now partly met by batteries.
questions: How can demand stay above secure minimum levels with millions of rooftop systems connected?
How do home and grid-scale batteries reshape evening peaks and prices?
Which services replace what large spinning generators gave the grid?

numbers.text: Renewables made 44.3% of NEM generation in July to September 2026, a record for that quarter (41.8% a year earlier).
NEM-wide minimum operational demand fell to an all-time low of 9,422 MW on Sunday 20 September 2026.
Rooftop and other distributed solar averaged 3,203 MW in July to September 2026, a record for that quarter.
4,562,198 small-scale solar systems installed across Australia, 30,917,812 kW of rated output, as of 30 September 2026 (all of Australia, not only the NEM).
